title: Ten open questions for elliptic curve index calculus
scope: The ranking prioritizes potential changes to attack complexity and concrete leads in the connected aburan28/cryptanalysis repository and its prime-field companion repositories. It is a research prioritization, not a consensus ranking. Established theoretical problems and repo-derived questions are labeled separately.
definitions: Prime-field curves are E(F_p) for prime p. Binary curves are ordinary curves over F_(2^n), with emphasis on prime n. Koblitz means binary subfield curves defined over F_2 and used over F_(2^n), a subset of binary curves. The prime-field j = 0 curve secp256k1 is included in the prime-field scope even though it is sometimes called a Koblitz curve. Throughout, r is the prime DLP subgroup order, n is an extension degree, m is the summand count, B is the actual usable factor-base point count, and C is the effective number of relation-matrix columns.
evidence: Repository results are reported as committed measurements, controls or conjectures. Published papers were checked at their primary pages or author manuscripts. The recent sources include the 2023 solving-degree paper, the 2024 Safe Curves survey and annealing paper, and September 2026 Hamming-ideal and annealing papers. Older 2020–2021 papers define construction and Frobenius questions that remain relevant. This synthesis adds no new measured attack or proof.
current_state: The reviewed evidence establishes no practical classical index-calculus improvement on the cryptographic prime-field or prime-degree binary/Koblitz instances considered here. Generic square-root lower bounds constrain black-box algorithms; they do not prove that coordinate-based index calculus is impossible. The repo's October 1, 2026 status note explicitly disclaims an ECDLP speedup from its volcano experiments.
solved_boundary: Frobenius acceleration itself is already established: Galbraith et al. obtain, under their conditions, about n fewer collected relations and an n^2 saving in final relation algebra. The unresolved issue is whether usable decompositions and the rest of the pipeline make those reductions competitive with Frobenius-accelerated rho. The shifted-base m! mechanism is also prior work, and the linearized two-point splitting idea has prior art.

questions.title: Can prime-field curves admit a sparse factor base with genuinely cheap decomposition?
questions.question: For a nonspecial E(F_p) subgroup of order r, can a coordinate-defined factor base support enough efficiently found m-point relations to make complete classical index calculus asymptotically faster than square-root search?
questions.basis: The prime-field repo's interval, multiplicative-subgroup, lattice and p-adic experiments expose obstacles in those particular constructions. Its Hecke follow-up also identifies designated relations that additive-closure or Fourier tests would miss. Published prime-field algebraic methods remain limited by decomposition and polynomial solving.
questions.open: Find a target-independent decomposition algorithm, rather than assume a free oracle. A null closure test is not a proof against every non-generic construction. A base of size r^(1/3) and fast relation generation alone do not establish a speedup: final relation solving and target recovery must also fit the budget.
questions.resolution: Give a parameterized family, an explicit membership and decomposition algorithm, a natural-query success estimate, and costs for relation rank, matrix solving and target recovery. For an experimental lead, freeze unseen targets and compare the measured exponent against tuned rho.

questions.title: What is the actual solving degree of binary summation systems as the parameters grow?
questions.status: Theoretical open problem with repo evidence
questions.question: Can one prove, or reliably characterize, how the solving degree grows with extension degree n, base dimension l and summand count m in the regimes that could improve ECDLP complexity?
questions.basis: Caminata and Gorla distinguish solving degree from first fall degree and related invariants. The repo measures a strong two-summand degree predictor, but labels its degree-131 table as a structural extrapolation and has no corresponding large-parameter m >= 3 result.
questions.open: A small first fall degree, bounded input degree, or a fit at fixed small m does not prove efficient solving when n and m grow together. Satisfiable and unsatisfiable ordinary queries can behave differently.
questions.resolution: Establish bounds for a specified formulation and monomial order, including field equations; then test held-out larger systems and retain censored queries. An m = 5 or 6 result needs its own evidence.

questions.title: Can Frobenius orbit decomposition retain a compact algebraic witness?
questions.question: Can a low-degree or sparse correspondence represent addition among signed Frobenius orbits while keeping only a small certificate of relative phases?
questions.basis: Galbraith et al. already establish Frobenius-based reductions in relation count and final matrix size. The repo's phase-eliminated quotient experiment found that all eight n = 19 target predicates needed degree 9 on its valid-key domain, exactly the degree where every Boolean function on that domain became representable.
questions.open: That negative result applies to the tested coordinates and fully eliminated predicate. Retained relative phases, nonlinear presentations and auxiliary-variable correspondences remain candidates. Orbit folding reduces the number of log unknowns; it does not automatically remove the witness search.
questions.resolution: Construct an exact quotient correspondence, independently lift its witnesses to curve points, and measure ordinary-query cost and independent-row yield on the same frozen base.

questions.title: Which Frobenius-stable nonlinear factor bases keep both yield and decomposition cost favorable?
questions.status: Repo-derived research direction informed by a recent paper
questions.question: Can nonlinear stable bases combine many usable subgroup points, few orbit columns and cheap membership constraints without moving the cost into auxiliary variables or phase search?
questions.basis: The repo combines normal-basis Hamming constraints with the factorized-convolution formulation of La Scala et al. (September 2026) in a complete degree-9 toy IC pipeline. The paper itself concerns syndrome decoding. The repo records no corresponding scaling result at degrees 53, 83 or 131 for that FC-Hamming method.
questions.open: Frobenius invariance and a bounded-degree Hamming encoding are useful ingredients, but their interaction with Semaev equations, actual subgroup density and ordinary-query solver difficulty is unsettled. Hamming weight is not the same as a linear factor-base subspace.
questions.resolution: Compare exact point sets and encodings on identical inputs, and measure setup, auxiliary-variable count, failed-query cost, useful rank and one-target recovery. Retain the existing weight encoding as a matched control.

questions.title: Can explicit quasi-subfield constructions become useful at prime extension degrees?
questions.question: Are there explicit quasi-subfield polynomial families at the desired prime n whose rational roots yield a usable factor base and a complete attack better than the current alternatives?
questions.basis: Huang et al. propose quasi-subfield factor bases. Euler and Petit provide further families and an existence limitation, while explicitly reporting no resulting speedup over prior ECDLP approaches. The repo's explicit-base frontier illustrates why actual usable point counts are essential.
questions.open: The desired regime requires enough rational roots, subgroup-valid points and affordable decomposition. A root-set size or tuple-count upper bound does not establish natural relation yield. Extension-field constructions do not directly give prime-field smallness.
questions.resolution: Supply a parameter family meeting all construction hypotheses, prove or measure its usable point count and natural success rate, and account for building the base and solving its relations.

questions.title: Can multi-summand formulations avoid paying back their degree reduction during lifting?
questions.question: Can symmetric coordinates, chained S3 equations or hybrid solvers find verified ordinary m-point decompositions faster than existing methods after splitting and membership checks are charged?
questions.basis: The repo shows that symmetric two-summand equations can be linear while the remaining affine solution space is expensive to enumerate. Three-summand behavior depends strongly on the factor-base product spaces. Its linearized-half method improves a decomposition stage without producing a rho-beating complete attack.
questions.open: Solving for elementary symmetric values does not guarantee that the associated polynomial splits into base coordinates with a valid group relation. Planted systems test correctness and satisfiable cost; they do not price ordinary relation collection.
questions.resolution: Use independently labeled ordinary and planted corpora at increasing m and l. Count all splitting, sign, rationality, subgroup and failed-query work, and compare direct, chained and symmetric formulations on the same base.

questions.title: How can a collector buy independent rank and reliable target descent efficiently?
questions.fields: Prime fields, binary fields and Koblitz curves
questions.question: Which witness selection, partial-relation recombination and stopping policies minimize cost per new rank contribution and per independently recovered target log?
questions.basis: The repo's monitor separates relation hits, attainable rank and descended targets. Its shifted-base audit records increased geometric coverage without a demonstrated faster collector. The published subfield framework also requires a usable relation matrix before recovery.
questions.open: Many hits can be duplicates or dependent, and quotient or cofactor structure can create a known nullspace. More coverage alone need not accelerate target recovery. Final relation algebra is modulo r, even when the PDP solver works over F_2.
questions.resolution: Freeze the query stream and rank checkpoints; compare collectors by rank gained per unit work, include partial-relation graph costs, and verify fresh-target descent. State how unavoidable kernels and anchors are handled.

questions.title: Can isogeny and Hecke mechanisms overcome their rank and transport barriers?
questions.fields: Prime fields; binary and Koblitz transport variants
questions.question: Can a concrete transport or correspondence produce enough cheap, independent relations to improve the DLP, including any links needed between modular isogeny classes?
questions.basis: The prime-field LEADS file verifies toy Hecke relations but reports substantial rank deficiency in its class-walk model. Those ranks use a proxy modulus, so they are not a theorem about every DLP subgroup. The binary volcano study reports nearly identical attempt counts for its source and descendants.
questions.open: For the Hecke mechanism, persistence of the deficit at deeper smooth conductors and a useful class-connecting relation are conjectural. For curve transport, an explicit isogeny preserves the DLP when its degree is coprime to r; any gain must come from a cheaper target representation after route costs.
questions.resolution: Recheck rank modulo the actual subgroup prime, prove the appropriate kernel dimension, and charge explicit map and target-transport costs. Compare complete same-target runs rather than infer a benefit from a changed conductor or j-invariant.

questions.title: Can a higher-genus cover make the elliptic component cheaper to solve?
questions.fields: Prime fields and binary fields, including Koblitz curves
questions.question: Can a cover or Jacobian construction preserve the desired elliptic subgroup and yield cheaper relation collection and target recovery for that component?
questions.basis: The repo has a tiny prime-field quartic norm-projection diagnostic and binary cover transfer infrastructure. It explicitly distinguishes norm relations on E from relations in the full Jacobian, where a Prym component can remain. Diem and Thome's genus-three index calculus supplies a relevant higher-genus benchmark.
questions.open: A map certificate is not an attack advantage. The genus-three heuristic O-tilde(q) bound is faster than rho for a group of size about q^3, but is larger than square-root search on a same-field elliptic subgroup of size about q.
questions.resolution: Prove pullback injectivity on the chosen subgroup, provide exact norm or pushforward operations and valid target lifts, identify the required E-component rank, and price the full pipeline against elliptic rho in the original field.

questions.title: Where is the verified complete-attack crossover with tuned Pollard rho?
questions.fields: Prime fields, binary fields and Koblitz curves
questions.question: For a precisely specified family, can any current algebraic, SAT, hybrid or quantum-annealing IC method recover an unseen target faster than tuned rho under comparable resources, and does the advantage persist as size increases?
questions.basis: The repo's benchmark distinguishes one-target online recovery from reusable setup and cold cost. The 2024 Edwards annealing paper reports a tiny F_1021 example; Lin et al.'s September 2026 paper reports a 16-bit prime-field demonstration. These sizes do not establish an asymptotic or cryptographic-size advantage.
questions.open: The target-dependent PDP, final relation solving when required, descent, verification, memory and failure distribution must be priced coherently. Koblitz rho must receive its signed-Frobenius benefit, and prime-field j = 0 or 1728 curves need their applicable automorphism controls.
questions.resolution: Run repeated same-point comparisons over a frozen size ladder and held-out tier. Report online one-target time as primary, reusable preprocessing and cold totals separately, and multi-target workloads with their own target count. For annealing, include embedding, classical preprocessing, readout and repetitions; establish scaling rather than extrapolate a small demonstration.

graph_audit: Checked the volcano figure inventory (census.svg, ecdlp.svg and tau.png), its canonical analyze.py source and results/summary.json; the factor-base degree/yield figures referenced by pdp-degree-heuristics; and the curve and isogeny route registries. This is a synthesis with no new curve, route or corrected measurement. Existing graph facts remain current. The new pipeline diagram and attempt-ratio plot explain the reviewed evidence and do not alter canonical graph sources.
curve_context: The principal full-width Koblitz reference is EC1N131Ckb1h136f03e58c98: y^2 + xy = x^3 + 1 over F_2[z]/(z^131 + z^13 + z^2 + z + 1), cofactor 4, subgroup order 680564733841876926932320129493409985129. The registered degree-263 descendant is EC1N131Cbinh833014327b07 and the verified route is IW1E263d1hadee4e69fa3d. Neither a route certificate nor these research proposals is a measured full-width IC candidate. The quantitative plot uses the legacy n = 19 volcano study, not a new EC1 or run ID.
plot_caption: Committed n = 19 study: E0/descendant mean PDP-attempt ratio = 0.9964, reported 95% interval [0.9765, 1.0166], from 31 curves x 10 scalars with 310/310 verified logs. A ratio of 1 means equal attempts; below 1 favors E0. The interval includes 1. This is an attempt-count result, not a wall-time or IC-versus-rho speedup. The interval is reproduced from the repository summary, not recomputed from raw trials.
next_work: For the next bounded repo experiment, prioritize questions 2, 3, 6 and 7: a frozen ordinary-query panel with an exact base, a solver-independent witness check and rank accounting can distinguish a useful algorithmic lead from a faster planted-system solve.
